newsitem.title: BRAZIL: New plant to make Fiat top LatAm carmaker.
newsitem.headline: New plant to make Fiat top LatAm carmaker.

text.p: Fiat SpA's new Argentine assembly plant, slated to begin output late this year, will allow it to displace rival Volkswagen AG as Latin America's top carmaker, the firm's regional chief said.

Giovanni Razelli, Fiat's superintendent for Argentina and Brazil, said that the new plant in Cordoba will enable the Italian auto giant to boost its total output in the two countries to 3,000 cars a day.
"We will produce our first car in Cordoba on December 20th," Razelli told Reuters in an interview.
He added that the plant, which will produce the compact sedan model of Fiat's new Palio, will reach output capacity of 1,000 cars a day sometime late next year.
A spokesman for Volkswagen do Brasil declined to respond directly to the Fiat claim it would overtake the German auto mammoth in the region.
"Whatever happens, the market will decide," he said.
Fiat Automoveis SA, the Italian firm's Brazilian unit and its biggest subsidiary outside Italy, is Brazil's top exporter and its third-largest firm based on 1995 sales of $6.23 billion.
The auto firm is now operating near capacity at a rate of 1,900 to 2,000 cars a day at its Betim plant in Minas Gerais state, officials said.

Razelli said production just in Brazil is expected to grow to 480,000 vehicles this year and climb to nearly 520,000 in 1997. Last year, output at Fiat Automoveis dipped to 463,893 cars from 500,738 in 1994.
By comparison, Volkwagen manufactured 604,347 vehicles last year in Brazil and Argentina and projects output this year to reach 720,000 vehicles, the firm's spokesman said.

Meanwhile, Fiat's sales, boosted by the introduction of its new Palio passenger car this year, are expected to rise to 430,000 vehicles for 1996 and 450,000 for 1997, he added. Last year, sales reached 417,091 automobiles.

Exports, which reached 132,781 cars in 1995, are seen steady this year and rising in 1997 to 150,000, Razelli said. Fiats produced in Brazil are exported to Argentina, Chile and other Latin American countries.
The automaker, which has invested close to $500 million this year, plans another $1.5 billion in investment in the region over the next three years.

But Razelli said expansion in Latin America is "conditioned on expansion and further integration of Mercosur," the customs union made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay with Chile as an associate.
Among possible new investments in Brazil is a $400 million engine plant. The plant would begin operating in 1998 or 1999 and produce 16-valve motors for the Mercosur market, he said.
Fiat does not have a presence in Mexico but hopes to set up a base there after the turn of the century, provided Mercosur and the three-nation North American Free Trade Area (NAFTA) reach an accord.
"In the future, Mexico will be an interesting country for us," he said.
